♻ ☆ Competition and Diversity in Generative AI
Manish Raghavan
Recent evidence, both in the lab and in the wild, suggests that the use of generative artificial intelligence reduces the diversity of content produced. The use of the same or similar AI models appears to lead to more homogeneous behavior. Our work begins with the observation that there is a force pushing in the opposite direction: competition. When producers compete with one another (e.g., for customers or attention), they are incentivized to create novel or unique content. We explore the impact competition has on both content diversity and overall social welfare. Through a formal game-theoretic model, we show that competitive markets select for diverse AI models, mitigating monoculture. We further show that a generative AI model that performs well in isolation (i.e., according to a benchmark) may fail to provide value in a competitive market. Our results highlight the importance of evaluating generative AI models across the breadth of their output distributions, particularly when they will be deployed in competitive environments. We validate our results empirically by using language models to play Scattergories, a word game in which players are rewarded for answers that are both correct and unique. Overall, our results suggest that homogenization due to generative AI is unlikely to persist in competitive markets, and instead, competition in downstream markets may drive diversification in AI model development.
♻ ☆ Semantic Alignment Between Normative Theories of Ethics and the European Union Artificial Intelligence Act: A Transformer-Based Semantic Textual Similarity Analysis
Mehmet Murat Albayrakoglu, Mehmet Nafiz Aydin
The European Union Artificial Intelligence (EU AI) Act, which explicitly references fundamental rights and ethical principles, is a comprehensive regulatory framework for governing Artificial Intelligence (AI) systems. This study examines the Act's possible moral grounding by analyzing the semantic alignment between three normative theories of ethics--virtue ethics, deontological ethics, and consequentialism--and the Act's regulatory language. Drawing on the philosophy of law, in which both antipositivist and some positivist accounts recognize an overlap between moral and legal norms, the relationship between the theories and the Act is treated as one of association. The encyclopedic descriptions of the theories serve as source documents, and the Act serves as the target document, analyzed in two target sections: its preamble and its statutory provisions. Semantic Textual Similarity (STS) is used as an indicator of association. The source documents are manually preprocessed to reduce semantic overlap among them. In all documents, each sentence is encoded by eight Transformer-based sentence encoders (SBERT, ALBERT, DistilBERT, RoBERTa, TinyBERT, MiniLM, E5-base, and GTE-base), and embeddings are aggregated to the document level by centroid cosine similarity, hierarchical sentence-block aggregation (HSBA; blocks of 3, 5, and 10 sentences), and mean pairwise sentence similarity. Because raw similarity scales differ across encoders, encoders are combined by voting on rankings. Deontological ethics shows the highest association with both target sections in all eight encoders and under every aggregation method, and the preamble is more closely associated with every source document than the provisions are. Consequentialism ranks second at the document level, but its position relative to virtue ethics depends on the granularity of aggregation.

♻ ☆ The Effect of Expertise Signaling when Sharing Medical Information in Opinion Dynamics
Moyi Li, Chuqiao Yan, Jesus Jair Reyes Gutierrez, Aleksandra Urman, Stefania Ionescu

This work investigates how signaling source expertise shapes trust and long-term opinion formation. Through an online experiment, we find that adding a professional title to the sender's display name significantly increases a post's perceived credibility. Incorporating these findings to create a data-driven opinion dynamics model, we prove that (1) connecting users through some paths to an expert guarantees consensus with experts' opinion, while (2) higher rates of expertise signaling accelerate reaching consensus. Simulations show that (3) convincing even 20% of users to signal their title reduces consensus time to nearly one-third in Erdos-Renyi networks and (4) higher title adoption brings average opinion much closer to that of experts in scale-free and real-world networks. Altogether, our work highlights expertise signaling as a viable intervention to promote validated medical information online.
♻ ☆ What Drives Students' Use of AI Chatbots? Technology Acceptance in Conversational AI
Griffin Pitts, Sanaz Motamedi
Conversational AI tools have been rapidly adopted by students and are becoming part of their learning routines. This widespread use comes amid ongoing concerns about the reliability of AI-generated responses and the appropriate role of AI in education. Drawing on the Technology Acceptance Model, we examine how students' perceptions of conversational AI, including its usefulness, ease of use, trustworthiness, enjoyment, and social influence, relate to their intentions to use these tools for learning. We investigate both the direct and indirect relationships among these perceptions to understand how they are associated with students' behavioral intentions. Using survey data from 229 students and partial least squares structural equation modeling, we found that perceived usefulness was the strongest direct predictor of intention, followed by perceived enjoyment. Perceived ease of use, trust, and subjective norms did not have significant direct associations with intention. However, trust and subjective norms had significant total indirect associations, while perceived enjoyment had both significant direct and indirect associations. The model explained 70.2% of the variance in behavioral intention. These findings suggest that students' intentions to use conversational AI are associated less directly with effort-related considerations and more with perceived usefulness and affective experience. They also highlight the importance of understanding what students perceive as valuable in conversational AI interactions, particularly when designing tools intended to encourage engagement while supporting learning.
♻ ☆ Delegations as Adaptive Representation Patterns: Rethinking Influence in Liquid Democracy
Davide Grossi, Andreas Nitsche
Liquid democracy is a mechanism for the division of labor in decision-making through the transitive delegation of influence. In essence, all individuals possess the autonomy to determine the issues with which they will engage directly, while for other matters, they may appoint a representative of their choosing. So far, the literature has studied the delegation structures emerging in liquid democracy as static. As a result, transitivity defined as the capacity to transfer acquired authority to another entity, has been identified as a concern as it would be conducive to unrestrained accumulation of power. Focusing on the implementation of liquid democracy supported by the LiquidFeedback software, we propose a novel approach to assessing the influence of voting nodes in a transitive delegation graph, taking into account the process nature of real-world liquid democracy in which delegation and voting are distinct and increasingly independent activities. By introducing a novel model of delegations in liquid democracy, we show how transitivity may in fact contribute to an effective regulation of deliberation influence and decision-making power. While maintaining the one-person, one-vote paradigm for all votes cast, the anticipated influence of an agent, to the extent it is stemming from transitivity, experiences a precipitous decline following an exponential trajectory. In general, it is our objective to move the first steps towards a rigorous analysis of liquid democracy as an adaptive democratic representation process. The adaptivity aspect of liquid democracy has not yet been explored within the existing academic literature despite it being, we believe, one of its most important features. We therefore also outline a research agenda focusing on this aspect of liquid democracy.

Arbaaz Muslim, Aviv Slobodkin, Katherine Wheeler-Martin, Eric Zhou, John Brittain, Martin Frasch, Hamsa Subramaniam, Jacob Bien, Hamed Sadeghi, Sarah Conderino, Stone Jiang, Ben Spoer, Daniel Neill, Mimi Sun, Joydeep Paul, Yun Liu, Tomer Shekel, Amy Chung-Yu Chou, Anna Carter, Charles Elliott, Aaron Bell, Reuven Sayag, Avinatan Hassidim, Niv Efron, Yossi Matias, Kasumi Widner, Eduardo Lopez Ortiz, José Alberto Díaz-Quiñonez, Moritz U. G. Kraemer, John Brownstein, Isaias Fernandes Co, Etien Luc Koua, Monica Bharel, Benjamin Rader, Lorna Thorpe, Marc Gourevitch, Shravya Shetty, Gautam Prasad
The efficacy of traditional disease prediction is limited by spatial gaps and temporal lags, which impact the timing and targets of resource deployments. Outbreaks escalate undetected, chronic disease burdens are quantified years later, and at-risk populations in data-sparse regions remain unaddressed. Planetary geospatial foundation models complement existing epidemiological workflows to provide operational improvements, encoding multimodal search, mobility, and environmental signals into generalizable place representations. As illustrations of this complementarity, we present independent global health case studies of Google Earth AI's Population Dynamics Foundation Model (PDFM) -- a foundation model for geospatial inference -- across four domains (vaccine-preventable, communicable, noncommunicable, maternal mental health), five tasks (spatial extrapolation, interpolation/nowcasting, probabilistic forecasting, prospective forecasting, risk stratification), and four countries (USA, Canada, Mexico, and the Democratic Republic of the Congo). Across these case studies, PDFM addresses critical surveillance gaps across domains: improving US-Canada border MMR vaccination coverage predictions by capturing cross-border behavioral spillovers domestic models miss; nowcasting cardiovascular disease to accelerate data availability; enhancing short-term municipal Mexican dengue forecasts for timely outbreak vector control; improving forecasts of cholera hotspots; and adding a transferable signal to individual-level postpartum-depression risk prediction in US states the model had never seen, while not replacing individual socioeconomic data or closing demographic screening gaps. Together, these results showcase capabilities of geospatial foundation models for public health surveillance.

☆ Source Attribution and Audience Uptake in Digital Witnessing: Evidence from a Chinese Diaspora Account on X
Huiqian Lai, Runze Ding

Less is known about audience uptake after publication and whether the attributed source corresponds to the form of response. This study analyzes 47,635 posts (April 2022 to May 2026) from Teacher Li Is Not Your Teacher, a diaspora-based account that curates and publishes reports and testimony from inside China for transnational audiences. Among 25,093 witness-relevant posts, 3,601 explicitly attribute their material to ordinary submitters. These posts receive more replies than other witness-relevant posts across adjusted analyses and show a more reply-oriented profile. The primary doubly robust retweet estimate is near zero. Among audited replies to November 2022 user-submitted posts, 91.4% substantively engage the focal material. The pattern is consistent with ordinary-person source attribution presenting testimony as situated and open to public response. The study extends digital witnessing beyond visibility by separating redistribution from the public response that gathers around testimony.

☆ How exposed is work to robotics? Occupational, industry, and geographic measures
Sebastian Sartor, Robert Seamans, Neil Thompson
Exposure indices that map technical capabilities onto occupational abilities have become a standard tool for anticipating how AI may reshape work, but existing measures either cover software AI or proxy robotics through patents and installation data that reflect the industrial robots of past decades. We construct the first abilities-based exposure measures for robotics and physical AI, and the first to span occupations, industries, and geographies. Following the framework of Felten et al. (2018, 2021), we build a robotics capability taxonomy of 16 capabilities in eight domains from 78 academic, industry, and standards sources, use a large language model to score the relatedness of each capability to the 52 ONET work abilities, and aggregate to Robotics Occupational Exposure (ROE) for 774 occupations, Robotics Industry Exposure (RIE) for 250 NAICS industries, and county-level Robotics Geographic Exposure (RGE). We find that robotics exposure concentrates in physically intensive work such as construction, farming, transportation, and production, and in industries such as logging, mining, trucking, and warehousing. Unlike generative-AI exposure, ROE is higher in occupations with lower wages, lower education requirements, and less creative-ability content. Physical collaboration and assistance, terrain-based locomotion, grasping and handling, and task and functional reasoning move the exposure ranking most, yet no single capability carries the index. Because the measures capture technical relatedness rather than readiness, cost, or adoption, they should be read as an upper bound on where physical automation could affect work.
☆ Desirability Confirmation: Relational Sycophancy in AI Intimate Roleplay
Huiqian Lai, Runze Ding
Research on LLM sycophancy has largely focused on propositional agreement, in which models echo users' beliefs, preferences, or judgments. Adult intimate roleplay presents a different case because what the user seeks may be preservation of a preferred relational position within a generated scene. Using a controlled prompt-based audit of 2,016 outputs from two open-weight LLMs, we identify four recurrent relational moves: legitimating desire, presenting the user as wanted, preserving non-rejection while communicating limits, and keeping intimacy available within fantasy or roleplay frames. Bringing the sycophancy literature into dialogue with sexual script theory, we conceptualize this configuration as desirability confirmation, an output-level pattern that captures how user-pleasing can operate through relational positioning. The findings extend sycophancy research and intimate-AI evaluation beyond binary compliance or refusal by showing how outputs can differ in the ways they communicate boundaries, preserve relational acceptance, and mark intimacy as fictional.

Panagiotis Kourtesis, Dante O'Connor, Sarah E. MacPherson

Before their scores are interpreted, the individuals they are intended to assess should find them usable, acceptable and tolerable, and for older adults this evidence is usually missing. This study evaluated the experience of the Trail Making Test in Virtual Reality (TMT-VR), a head-gaze adaptation of the Trail Making Test that requires no hand-held controller, in 47 younger (20-38 years) and 44 older adults (64-81 years). After the task, participants rated usability, pragmatic and hedonic user experience, acceptability, and cybersickness. The study had three aims: to compare the two age groups on these ratings; to examine whether the ratings were associated with age group, gaming and technology experience, and whether cybersickness was associated with motion sickness susceptibility; and to examine whether the ratings were related to TMT-VR completion and error-adjusted times. Both groups rated the TMT-VR as highly usable, acceptable and pleasant to use. Older adults gave slightly lower usability and pragmatic ratings, but neither the age-group differences nor the associations with age group or previous experience were statistically significant after correction. Cybersickness was low, with 38 of the 91 participants reporting no symptoms; it did not differ between the age groups and was not associated with motion sickness susceptibility. No correlation between the ratings and TMT-VR performance survived correction. The TMT-VR with head-gaze selection is therefore usable, acceptable and well tolerated by older as well as younger adults. Because the ratings were favourable across the whole range of TMT-VR scores, slower or less accurate performance is unlikely to reflect difficulty with the interface.

☆ Over reliant and underprepared: First responder resilience to disruption of operational technology
James Connor, Courtney Crooks, Ryan Shandler
The Emergency Services Sector (ESS) is responsible for taking life-saving action in the face of extreme crises. To enhance its response capabilities, the sector has spent the last two decades investing in new technology to improve their operational efficiency. This has created significant interdependencies and a culture among first responders of technical overreliance, raising questions about what would occur if those tools were suddenly disrupted. Several works have discussed the potential for terrorism to intentionally target ESS technology as part of a larger kinetic attack. Despite this, the resilience of first responder agencies to technological disruption and their preparedness for such an attack has largely remained unexplored. To bridge this gap, we implemented a novel scenario-based interview methodology involving senior officials from emergency service agencies across the United States. These interviews explored how each agency prepared for a disruption of operational technology and what factors might influence different levels of preparation between them. Participants were asked to describe their responses to a hypothetical scenario modeled after historical cyber-attacks against ESS infrastructure. The results indicate that while ESS agencies are prepared for short-term technological disruptions, they are likely to struggle with long-term or hybrid incidents. The data further revealed that agencies often lack dedicated expertise in cybersecurity, technology, and emergency management that could otherwise elevate resilience to interruptions of operational technology. These findings emphasize the need for investment in redundant analog systems, increased training for frontline personnel, and a focused effort against loss of specialized technical expertise among ESS agencies.

☆ Bad Diagnosis: Analyzing Consent and Data Collection Practices of Mobile Medical Apps
Ethan Myers, Lorenzo De Carli, Shantanu Sharma, Ritwik Banerjee, Joel Reardon, Indrakshi Ray
Mobile health (mHealth) apps collect personally-identifiable information while handling uniquely sensitive medical data, ranging from mental health records to real-time glucose or heart rate monitoring -- yet they remain poorly understood at scale. We present the first comprehensive analysis of consent and data collection practices across 10,000+ mHealth apps on the Google Play Store, combining static analysis and privacy policy examination. We develop a rigorous operational definition to distinguish health apps from general wellness programs, and design a measurement framework to detect misuse of permissions and violations of consent. Our analyses reveal a troubling ecosystem: 69.15% of apps request at least one permission unrelated to their stated purpose, with over 52.9% apps requesting location data, and 50.5% and 34.9% apps requesting camera and microphone access, respectively -- despite no functional justification based on app descriptions and stated purposes. Most alarmingly, nearly 93% of apps fail to provide users with a consent form, directly violating regulatory requirements such as GDPR; and even among the remaining 7%, 1 in 14 demonstrate a gap between the obtained consent and collection of personally identifiable information. These findings demonstrate an urgent need for stronger enforcement of privacy regulations in mHealth apps. We plan to release our dataset and measurement tools for continued monitoring of this critical space.

We address this gap for Chinese names, which appear in two forms, Hanzi and Pinyin, its Romanized form (e.g., Zhang Wei, Li Na). However, a single pinyin name can correspond to multiple distinct hanzi characters with different gender associations, so gender inference from Pinyin alone is intrinsically ambiguous. To address this, we first develop two hanzi models, a regression model that produces a continuous gender score from 0 (male) to 1 (female), and a classification model that outputs one of three labels (\em{male}, \em{neutral}, \em{female}). We train them on a sample of hanzi names from Chinese-language physics publications, rated by 11 native Chinese speakers. On this sample, the models achieve an RMSE of $0.09$ and an R$^2$ of $0.85$ (regression), and macro-AUC of $0.97$ and a Cohen's $κ$ of $0.81$ (classification), demonstrating high performance that is robust to class imbalance. For pinyin names, we propose a pipeline that aggregates hanzi predictions via transliteration and frequency weighting, together with an ambiguity score that flags names whose gender cannot be resolved from Pinyin alone. Benchmarked against three off-the-shelf tools (Namsor, GPT, and Claude), our models achieve the highest agreement with human annotations for both gender scores and gender labels, in both scripts. Applied to an independent sample of Chinese-named authors in APS journals, our models assign a gender to every name, whereas existing Pinyin-based methods leave between 20\% and 100\% of names unclassified. These findings demonstrate the importance of hanzi-level information for reliable gender inference of Chinese names. Code and data are publicly available.

☆ Water-Energy-Data nexus reveals sustainability gaps and priorities for AI infrastructure
Jincheng Huang, Guoan Xiao, Xin Lan, Caichun Yin, Zhimeng Jiang, Yue Cui, Jianguo Liu
The rapid growth of artificial intelligence (AI) depends on interconnected water, energy, and data systems spanning infrastructure life cycles and diverse geographies, with the potential to intensify water and energy insecurity, exacerbate social inequities and lead to cascading sustainability issues globally. Yet assessments commonly examine them separately, limiting our understanding of where resource pressures arise, how they are transferred across space, and who bears their consequences. To address these challenges, we established a water-energy-data (WED) nexus framework that captures the spatial and life-cycle dependencies of AI infrastructure, and use large language models to synthesize 12,825 water- or energy-related studies across four resource-intensive AI infrastructure activities: mineral extraction, semiconductor manufacturing, data center operation and electronic-waste processing. The evidence map identifies a mismatch between the interconnected activities supporting AI infrastructure and boundaries used to assess them. Researchers assess operational energy more than water use and other indirect demands, while interactions across locations and life-cycle activities remain understudied. These gaps obscure how resource demands shift among infrastructure nodes and regions, and how data-enabled benefits compare with their underlying costs. The WED nexus provides a foundation for integrated assessment of spatially metacoupled systems, while the evidence map can inform priorities for managing the sustainability implications of the AI boom.

This contradicts our preregistered hypothesis that the deficit would grow with forecast horizon. In a separate nine-seed experiment, directly supervising the uncorrected output reverses its precipitation forecast deficit at 72 hours while maintaining the accuracy of corrected forecasts at 24 hours. In ConCerNet's heat-equation system, projection-trained models have higher uncorrected trajectory-based vector-field RMSE than models trained without projection, while restoring the physical projection recovers accuracy far more effectively than a matched nonphysical control. Together, these results show that hard corrections can reshape the predictors trained alongside them, creating dependencies that are not visible from corrected forecasts alone. Hard-constrained emulators should therefore be evaluated by separately measuring predictor accuracy, correction effects, and their interaction during training.

Our results show that graphlet features complement event log counts in improving classification performance. Using SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP), we further derive model explanations that reveal method-specific graphlet structural patterns.

☆ TRACE: Governing AI-Assisted Research with Principles from Computer Science
Amirhossein Zohrehvand, Aldona Kapačinskaitė
Artificial intelligence (AI) makes it easier than ever to produce research outputs. The pressing question is how researchers should organize their work with this technology. The question is not new: software engineering and security research have long studied how teams of people and machines keep control of a shared body of work with many contributors. We distil principles from the practices these literatures report and transpose them to AI-assisted research. The principles form TRACE: Track records, Review against sources, Accept independently, Control transitions, and Evaluate corrections. Together, the five principles give researchers a common basis for remaining in control while integrating AI into their workflows. By bounding units of work and attending to how each is shaped, they help researchers pace AI-assisted work to human attention rather than to the speed at which AI produces content. We also introduce TRACE-OS, an open source operating system for AI-assisted research projects. It puts the principles into practice through shared instructions, tools, and records that fit researchers' existing workflows. The shared standard can contribute to building trust, which allows teams to delegate and realize the productivity that AI promises. More broadly, we aim to open a conversation about the governing principles through which the research community can benefit from AI.

☆ Regulating for an AI Commons: Adopting, sustaining, and defending people-first innovation trajectories
Abhineet Nayyar, Mallory Knodel, Kimberlee Weatherall, Gunn Jiravuttipong
Technological principles of openness, interoperability, and decentralization are integral to building an AI economy that is accountable to the public and truly responsive to local needs and constraints. However, Big Tech's firm control over essential elements of the stack (such as chips, cloud, models, data, and talent) limits valuable alternatives from reaching the scale necessary for sustained growth. Worse still, hyperscalers continue to enclose and extract value from publicly funded and volunteer-driven technologies without adequately distributing these returns. We see consolidated power within a few entities and "enshittification" of once-transformative innovations. Embedding ethical micro-level tools (like open data repositories or small-language models) into workflows is promising, but without a consistent innovation strategy, they also often end up perpetuating and being appropriated by the same exploitative trajectories. Instead, this whitepaper outlines a three-pillared holistic and intentional policy approach that i) actively pushes for the adoption of cooperative technologies in existing and emerging systems, ii) sets up collective institutional structures to sustain and maintain them in the long-term, and iii) introduces regulatory proposals that limit private entities from disempowering them through uncontrolled enclosure and extraction. Through desk research and purpose-specific case studies, we argue for the importance of such an approach in the Global South, where structural constraints around infrastructure, financing, and policy governance make it difficult for AI commons and cooperative AI tools to emerge and survive. The paper concludes with key open questions for campaigners, policy advocates, researchers, and grassroots organizers to consider and explore while working towards peoples' solidarity within and between Global South countries.
☆ Can AI interview? Comparing AI-led to Human-led Chat Interviews
Semra Guven, Tobias Gårdhus, Andreas Bjerre-Nielsen, Anna Rogers, Hjalmar Bang Carlsen
Large language model chatbots have been proposed as AI-interviewers for collecting qualitative interview data at scale, potentially bridging social science's longstanding divide between the breadth of surveys and the depth of qualitative interviews. This paper provides the first direct empirical comparison of data quality in AI-led and human-led interviews. In a randomized experiment (N = 41), university students were interviewed via synchronous text chat by either trained non-expert interviewers or a locally hosted AI system; we evaluate exposure, specificity, and relevance. Median interview duration was similar across conditions, but AI-interviewers asked more than twice as many questions per interview and elicited roughly 65 percent more respondent text per interview. Per-question responses were longer with human interviewers, though not after multiple-testing correction; only AI-condition participants skipped questions. Responses were almost uniformly on-topic in both conditions; for specificity we detect no difference, but the design cannot exclude one of up to three quarters of a point. These results were obtained with a small, locally hosted open-weight model (7B parameters), which addresses concerns about data security, GDPR compliance, and scientific reproducibility. Our findings support the viability of AI-interviewing for large-N qualitative data collection.

♻ ☆ Using Agency Law to Tame AI Agents
Deven R. Desai, Mark O. Riedl
Artificial Intelligence (AI) Agents have entered the marketplace. By some estimates, AI Agents, which promise to execute tasks and even take over your computer to do so, present a more than $400 billion market. The potential power of AI Agents has fueled legal scholars' fears that AI Agents will enable rogue commerce, human manipulation, rampant defamation, and infringement of intellectual property rights. These scholars are calling for regulation before AI Agents cause havoc. This Article addresses concerns about AI Agents head-on. The Article leverages the socio-legal issues presented by agency law to identify potential problems. It then asks how computer science can solve those problems rather than trying to take rules for humans and impose them on software. This approach shows that core aspects of modern software engineering, particularly client server architectures, address several of those concerns in ways quite different from---and arguably stronger than---how the law would discipline a human agent.

♻ ☆ Selective Data Expansion for Model Performance
Jahid Hasan, Romila Pradhan
Machine learning systems are increasingly being used in critical decision making such as healthcare, finance, and criminal justice. Concerns around their fairness have resulted in several bias mitigation techniques that emphasize the need for high-quality data to ensure fairer decisions. However, the role of earlier stages of machine learning pipelines in mitigating model bias has not been explored well. In this paper, we focus on the task of acquiring additional labeled data points for training the downstream machine learning model to rapidly improve its fairness. Since not all data points in a data pool are equally beneficial to the task of fairness, we generate an ordering in which data points should be acquired. We present DataSift, a data acquisition framework based on the idea of data valuation that relies on partitioning and multi-armed bandits to determine the most valuable data points to acquire. Over several iterations, DataSift selects a partition and randomly samples a batch of data points from the selected partition, evaluates the benefit of acquiring the batch on model fairness, and updates the utility of partitions depending on the benefit. To further improve the effectiveness and efficiency of evaluating batches, we leverage influence functions that estimate the effect of acquiring a batch without retraining the model. We empirically evaluate DataSift on several real-world and synthetic datasets and show that the fairness of a machine learning model can be significantly improved even while acquiring a few data points.

♻ ☆ Bridging the Gap in the Responsible AI Divides
Bálint Gyevnár, Atoosa Kasirzadeh
Tensions between AI Safety (AIS) and AI Ethics (AIE) have created what we term a "responsible AI divide." This divide has been persistent, and has dominated the public and policy discourse on AI, and increasingly shapes how governments, firms, and researchers define responsible AI, and so which AI risks they prioritize, which they sideline, and which mitigation strategies they ultimately develop and implement. Here, we first introduce categorization with four major conceptual modes of possible engagement with these tensions: radical confrontation, disengagement, compartmentalized coexistence, and critical bridging. Second, we discuss the advantages and disadvantages of the modes of engagement. Third, we empirically analyze a well-curated set of 3555 research papers roughly representing AIS and AIE. Using computational tools and qualitative analyses, we map the research landscapes of AIE and AIS. We observe that there are several shared research problems between AIE and AIS. However, there are also several thematic divides. For example, we find that AIE has long grappled with problems related to injustice incurred by AI and tangible AI harms, whereas AIS has primarily embodied an anticipatory approach focused on mitigating risks from AI capabilities. At the same time, we find significant overlap in core research concerns across AIE and AIS regarding transparency, reproducibility, and inadequate governance mechanisms. Based on our empirical observations, we claim that critical bridging, with a focus on bridging problems, offers one viable, constructive path for advancing responsible AI. We conclude by identifying bridging problems as a foundation for collaborative AI governance, offering concrete recommendations for integrating shared considerations into responsible AI practice, discussing the limitations of critical bridging, and outlining open problems for future research.
♻ ☆ Bonsai: A class of effective methods for independent sampling of graph partitions
Jeanne Clelland, Kristopher Tapp
We develop effective methods for constructing an ensemble of district plans via independent sampling from a reasonable probability distribution on the space of graph partitions. We compare the performance of our algorithms to that of standard Markov Chain based algorithms in the context of grid graphs and state congressional and legislative maps. For the case of perfect population balance between districts, we provide an explicit description of the distribution from which our method samples.
♻ ☆ MARTA Reach: Toward an On-Demand Multimodal Transit System in Atlanta
Pascal Van Hentenryck, Connor Riley, Anthony Trasatti, Hongzhao Guan, Tejas Santanam, Jorge A. Huertas, Kevin Dalmeijer, Kari Watkins, Juwon Drake, Samson Baskin
On-Demand Multimodal Transit Systems (ODMTS) adopt a transit-centric model, integrating fixed-route public transit with on-demand shuttles to provide integrated, door-to-door multimodal service. Although simulation studies have demonstrated the theoretical potential of ODMTS, the system has not yet been tested in practice at scale. In collaboration with the transit agency of the Atlanta metropolitan region (MARTA), the authors organized MARTA Reach, a six-month on-demand mobility pilot to explore the practical viability of ODMTS. Reach offered on-demand services across four different zones, connecting each zone to the existing transit network and offering an integrated flat fare. This allowed for testing key system components in real-world conditions. Ridership steadily increased throughout the pilot, suggesting potential for growth if a full ODMTS were implemented. Reach offered a highly valued service with 94% satisfaction rate, and 12.24% of survey respondents indicated they would have driven, ridden with someone, or taken a taxi or ride-hailing service otherwise. The vast majority of Reach trips were multimodal, especially in West Atlanta, where over 70% of morning riders connected to rail. The paper presents a potential path to economic viability and discusses practical challenges encountered during the pilot, along with strategies for future deployments. Following the pilot, MARTA officially adopted MARTA Reach as a long-term component of its transportation services in March 2026. The system-wide on-demand transit service currently serves 12 zones with the integrated flat fare and the organizational structure advocated in the pilot. The adoption decision demonstrates that the insights, system components, and operational lessons documented in this paper translated directly into a larger real-world deployment, providing an opportunity to evaluate ODMTS performance at scale.
♻ ☆ Queer NLP: A Critical Survey on Literature Gaps, Biases and Trends ACL
Sabine Weber, Angelina Wang, Ankush Gupta, Arjun Subramonian, Dennis Ulmer, Eshaan Tanwar, Geetanjali Aich, Hannah Devinney, Jacob Hobbs, Jennifer Mickel, Joshua Tint, Mae Sosto, Ray Groshan, Simone Astarita, Vagrant Gautam, Verena Blaschke, William Agnew, Wilson Y Lee, Yanan Long
Natural language processing (NLP) technologies are rapidly reshaping how language is created, processed, and interpreted by humans. With current and potential applications in hiring, law, healthcare, and other areas that impact people's lives, understanding and mitigating harms towards marginalized groups is critical. In this survey, we examine NLP research papers that explicitly address the relationship between LGBTQIA+ communities and NLP technologies. We systematically review all such papers published in the ACL Anthology up until February 2026 (n=122), to answer the following research questions: (1) What are current research trends? (2) What gaps exist in terms of topics and methods? (3) What areas are open for future work? We find that while the number of papers on queer NLP has grown within the last few years, most papers take a reactive rather than a proactive approach, focusing on shortcomings of existing systems rather than creating new solutions. Our survey uncovers many opportunities for future work, especially regarding stakeholder involvement, intersectionality, interdisciplinarity, and languages other than English. We also offer an outlook from a queer studies perspective, highlighting understudied topics and blind spots in the harms addressed in NLP papers. Beyond being a roadmap of what has been done, this survey is a call to action for work towards more just and inclusive NLP technologies.

♻ ☆ Learning from Convenience Samples: Fine-Tuning LLMs to Predict Voting Choices from Biased Survey Samples
Tobias Holtdirk, Dennis Assenmacher, Arnim Bleier, Claudia Wagner
Survey research increasingly relies on convenience samples as rising costs and nonresponse make representative probability sampling more difficult. This creates a central challenge for public opinion research and electoral studies: how to recover reliable population-level inferences from socially and demographically biased data. While recent work has explored the use of large language models (LLMs) for simulating survey responses, most studies focus on the U.S. population and assume relatively favourable data conditions with limited or random missingness. In this work, we investigate whether LLMs can leverage contextual knowledge about socio-demographic and political patterns to predict vote choice in the German population under sampling constraints. We systematically vary both the size and composition of training data, ranging from large representative samples to small, biased convenience samples, and compare zero-shot prompting and supervised fine-tuning against established tabular classifiers such as CatBoost. Our results show that when representative training data are available, fine-tuned LLMs achieve predictive performance comparable to strong tabular baselines and substantially outperform zero-shot prompting. Under small and biased convenience samples, however, fine-tuned LLMs more accurately recover both individual-level vote choice and population-level distributions than zero-shot approaches and often outperform tabular methods. These findings suggest that fine-tuned LLMs can combine sample-specific information with contextual knowledge acquired during pre-training, enabling more robust inference under conditions of sampling bias and missing data.

♻ ☆ Risk Ceilings and Development Deadlines: Pacing AI under Uncertain Safety Productivity
Li Gan
Can a regulator promise both a risk ceiling and a development deadline when safety productivity is unknown? A ceiling below the final model's unprotected hazard requires a minimum stock of safety knowledge, so both promises hold only if weak research can be ruled out. Learning first and then replaying development, with spare compute in safety, comes close to that minimum. In a calibration with only state risk, constant safety yield, and full knowledge transfer, it needs only 3.3 percent more productivity than the necessary bound. Customer services pay for the guarantee. Rules that fix compute allocation fix dates, not risk.

♻ ☆ A null model to detect coordinated online behavior integrating evidence from multiple indicators
Filipi Nascimento Silva, Manita Pote, Lake Yin, David Axelrod, Ashwin Balasubramanian, Luca Luceri, Filippo Menczer, Alessandro Flammini
Coordinated online accounts can amplify messages and manipulate attention, but detecting such behavior is challenging due to confounding factors like account activity and item popularity. We propose a statistical null-model framework that assesses behavioral similarity between accounts by comparing observed coordination indicators against activity- and popularity-conditioned reference distributions. By combining evidence across multiple indicators and partners, our method can identify suspicious coordination links more accurately. Evaluations on nine labeled information-operation datasets involving over 152 thousand accounts show that aggregating p-values multiplicatively across indicators and partners yields improved detection performance. While results vary across information operations, this approach offers a generalizable and statistically principled tool for uncovering coordinated online behavior.

♻ ☆ AI-exposed jobs deteriorated before ChatGPT
Morgan R. Frank, Alireza Javadian Sabet, Lisa Simon, Sarah H. Bana, Renzhe Yu
Public debate links worsening job prospects for AI-exposed occupations to the release of ChatGPT in late 2022. Using monthly U.S. unemployment insurance records, we measure occupation- and location-specific unemployment risk and find that risk rose in AI-exposed occupations beginning in early 2022, months before ChatGPT was released. Analyzing millions of LinkedIn profiles, we show that graduate cohorts from 2021 onward entered AI-exposed jobs at lower rates than earlier cohorts, with gaps opening before late 2022. Finally, from millions of university syllabi, we find that graduates taking more LLM-exposed curricula had shorter job searches after ChatGPT and higher first-job pay when entering highly exposed occupations. Together, these results---pointing to forces pre-dating generative AI and to the ongoing value of LLM-relevant education---suggest that generative AI may not be the root cause of these labor market hardships and that the launch of ChatGPT is a faulty natural experiment for understanding AI's impact on jobs.
♻ ☆ Happy Young Women, Grumpy Old Men? Emotion-Driven Demographic Biases in Synthetic Face Generation
Mengting Wei, Aditya Gulati, Guoying Zhao, Nuria Oliver
Synthetic faces from text-to-image (T2I) models pervade digital media, yet their demographic biases under emotionally conditioned prompts remain poorly understood. We aim to systematically audit how emotionally conditioned prompts affect demographic and perceived-attractiveness biases in synthetic faces generated by T2I models, with particular attention to intersectional patterns and cross-ecosystem differences across model families. We audited eight (4 Western and 4 Chinese) T2I models and generated 56,000 faces under seven prompt conditions: a neutral baseline and six emotion conditions. We quantified biases in gender, race, age, and perceived attractiveness using information-theoretic divergence metrics. We further conducted intersectional analyses across combined demographic attributes and compared patterns between the Western and Chinese model groups to assess cross-ecosystem consistency and divergence in bias behavior. All models show strong overrepresentation of young faces, and most also overrepresent White-coded individuals. Intersectional analysis reveals compound underrepresentation or near-erasure of specific demographic combinations, such as young x female x Black faces, which are largely absent across models and are not captured by single-attribute audits. Emotion prompts act as additional demographic selectors: negatively valenced emotions (including sadness and fear) consistently shift outputs toward White, middle-aged, male-coded faces. This produces a valence-driven mapping that is also associated with lower perceived attractiveness in generated faces. These findings indicate that demographic bias in T2I face generation is both pervasive and shaped by emotional conditioning. They underscore the need for intersectional, emotion-conditioned, and multilingual demographic audits as part of standard pre-deployment evaluation practices.

♻ ☆ Pro-AI Bias in Large Language Models
Benaya Trabelsi, Jonathan Shaki, Sarit Kraus
Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly employed for decision-support across multiple domains. We ask whether these models favor artificial intelligence (AI) itself. We examine this question through three experiments. First, in open-ended advice across investment, study, career, and startup domains, AI is prominent in most recommendation lists and is usually ranked first when it appears. Second, in salary estimations, models overestimate AI-related jobs more than they do for closely matched non-AI jobs. In a controlled follow-up, changing only the job title from the matched non-AI title to the AI-related title raises predicted salary by 10%, while all other supplied job details remain fixed. Finally, we show that the number of degrees and other credentials awarded by AI programs were 28% more overestimated than corresponding awards for matched computing programs. Overall, we show that AI is not only prominent in everyday LLM advice, but also receives systematically inflated quantitative estimates compared to non-AI cases, even against its closest disciplinary neighbors, raising concerns for high-stakes decision support.
